q: One French grand cru appellation covers exactly the ground of a single property, so the appellation boundary and the estate map are the same line. Which appellation?
exp: The appellation runs to a shade under two hectares in Vosne-Romanee and has not been divided in living memory, so a vintage yields one wine and one only. Echezeaux and Corton sit at the other extreme, each of them split among dozens of separate owners, and even Musigny, small as it is, is shared among a handful.

q: A narrow strip of vineyard runs straight up the slope between Romanee-Conti and La Tache, and every row of it has long been farmed by one family. Name that climat.
exp: It was left a premier cru when the grand crus of Vosne-Romanee were drawn up in the 1930s and was promoted only in 1992, late enough that older books still print it a rank below its neighbours. The name records an old road running up the hill rather than any claim about the wine, and the strip is narrow because it follows that route.

q: Clos Sainte Hune, a walled plot of a little over a hectare and a half at Hunawihr, lies inside one of Alsace's grand crus, though the label has traditionally said nothing about it. Name the grand cru.
exp: Rosacker is limestone and dolomite on the slope above Hunawihr, and the clos sits in the heart of it. The house behind the wine built its reputation long before the grand cru system was delimited at all, which is why the plot name has always carried more weight on that label than the site name would.

q: A wall dated 1698 encloses just under two hectares of Chardonnay in the middle of the village of Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, and the house that bought it in 1971 bottles the plot on its own in declared years. Name the clos.
accept: clos du mesnil blanc de blancs
clos du mesnil in le mesnil sur oger
exp: Being walled inside a village rather than open on the slope, it ripens a little differently from the vineyard around it, which is the whole argument for keeping it apart. A single-vineyard Champagne of this kind gives up the blender's usual insurance, so it appears only in years the plot can carry a wine by itself.

q: Above the Marne at Mareuil-sur-Ay a walled slope pitches at something close to forty-five degrees, the steepest planted ground in Champagne, and it has been bottled as a vintage wine in nearly every harvest since 1935. Name that clos.
accept: clos des goisses at mareuil sur ay
exp: The pitch and the due-south exposure ripen fruit well ahead of the villages around it, which is why the wine can be declared in years its neighbours would not. Goisses comes from a local word for a very steep slope, so the name describes the ground rather than the wine, and the wall marks a holding that has never been broken up.

q: A guest compares two vintages of one classified Medoc estate and finds the first blend led by Merlot and the second by Cabernet Sauvignon, although no vines were pulled up between them. What accounts for the swing?
opts: The estate replanted a large parcel and did not announce it
Lots that fell short of the grand vin were left out of it, and which variety fell short differs from one year to the next
Appellation rules fix a different blend for each vintage according to the season
The second wine takes a fixed share of every variety, so what remains sets the proportions
exp: Planting is a decision of decades and blending a decision of one winter, so the two never match. A wet September that spoils the Merlot and a cool one that leaves the Cabernet green both show up in the assemblage rather than in the vineyard, and an estate that kept its proportions fixed in spite of the season would be bottling its weather, not correcting for it.

q: Alsace's grand cru rules admit only one named site to a label, so a house whose long-lived Riesling cuvee is drawn from parcels in a pair of them prints no grand cru name at all. Which grand crus are blended in that cuvee?
accept: grand cru geisberg and grand cru osterberg
the geisberg and osterberg grand crus
exp: The pair sit side by side on the slope above Ribeauville, Geisberg the steeper and more terraced of them, and a blend across the two forfeits a mention that either could have carried alone. The house treats its own cuvee name as the stronger claim, which is a fair reading of how Alsace was actually sold before the grand crus were delimited.

q: One Champagne prestige cuvee is assembled from several declared vintages rather than from a single one, on the argument that a blend of good years beats the best of them alone, and it therefore carries no date. Name that cuvee.
exp: Each release blends years the house had declared as vintages in their own right, which reverses the usual assumption that a vintage wine outranks a blended one. The house now numbers each release as an iteration in its own sequence, and each is built from a different trio of those years rather than to a fixed recipe.

q: A dry white is pressed at the sole Premier Cru Superieur of Sauternes, from the same rows as its sweet wine, and it goes to market under a single letter of the alphabet. Name that wine.
accept: ygrec the dry white of yquem
exp: Ygrec is the French name of the letter Y, and the wine is a Sauvignon and Semillon blend from fruit picked before botrytis takes hold, or from a year in which it never does. It is not declassified sweet wine: the decision is taken at the start of the harvest rather than at the end of it, and the wine is fermented dry on purpose. Yquem stands alone as Premier Cru Superieur above the eleven first growths of 1855, several of which now press a dry white of their own under a single initial, R at Rieussec, S at Suduiraut and G at Guiraud.

q: Two adjoining Stags Leap District vineyards, S.L.V. and Fay, are normally bottled apart; in years when a barrel selection drawn from both is judged to beat either, one Napa winery releases a third wine instead. Name it.
accept: stag s leap wine cellars cask 23
exp: The wine began as a single cask set aside in 1974 and has been made only in vintages the cellar thinks justify it. Naming the source vineyards on their own labels and blending them for the flagship is the reverse of the Bordeaux habit, where the blend is the flagship and the parcels are never seen at all.

q: From the 2012 vintage one Pauillac first growth stopped offering its wine as futures and now releases each vintage when it judges the wine ready to drink. What changed for the buyer?
opts: It arrives a year earlier, before the final blend has been settled
Only the estate may sell it, the negociants of the Place having been cut out of the trade altogether
The estate's 1855 rank lapses on any vintage sold outside a futures campaign
It arrives years later, at a price set against the market of the day
exp: Selling futures moves the cash risk from the chateau to the buyer and the storage risk with it, and withdrawing reverses both. The estate holds the stock in its own cellars for a decade and releases in tranches, and the trade still handles the wine, so what disappeared is the barrel sale rather than the merchant.

q: A Cote des Blancs house has never made a non-vintage wine, a rose or a blend of villages, and in a year it does not care for it releases nothing at all under its name. Name that house.
accept: salon of le mesnil sur oger
exp: Fewer than fifty vintages have been released since the first in 1905, so in most years the fruit it has contracted goes elsewhere and no bottle appears. The wine is a blanc de blancs from one grand cru village, held far beyond the legal minimum before disgorgement, and the refusal to make anything else is the whole of the house's proposition.

q: One Champagne house releases the same vintage more than once: at around eight years, and then again after far longer on the lees, with every release presented as a further stage in that wine's life. What does the house call those stages?
exp: The argument is that a wine on its lees does not develop steadily but arrives at a series of windows, and the cellar disgorges at each of them rather than once. The later releases were sold for years under a different name borrowed from the house's own library before the current one was adopted, so old bottles and new ones carry both.

q: Growers in one Jura appellation submit their wine to a committee that may refuse the whole vintage, and when it does, not a bottle is sold under the name. Name that appellation.
exp: The appellation makes vin jaune and nothing else, and the wine spends more than six years in cask under a veil of yeast before it may be bottled, so a refusal falls on work long since done. Whole vintages were declassified outright in the 1970s and 1980s, and the rejected wine goes to market as plain Cotes du Jura instead.

q: Asked at the table what a Bordeaux second wine actually contains, a sommelier should be able to answer without guessing. What governs it?
opts: Fruit from a separate vineyard the estate keeps for the purpose, outside its classified holding
A share of the crop fixed by the appellation, which is why the proportion barely moves from one vintage to the next
The press wine, the free-run juice all going into the grand vin
Whatever the estate left out of its grand vin, most often young vines and parcels that underperformed
exp: Nothing in law fixes the category, so a second wine carries the same appellation as the grand vin and differs from it only by selection. Estates that once sold their surplus lots in bulk now bottle them, and several have added a third wine underneath, which is a commercial judgement about how far the selection can be pushed.

q: A Margaux third growth presents its junior label not as a strainer for lots that missed the grand vin but as a different reading of the same vineyard, picked and raised its own way. Name that wine.
exp: Palmer makes the point that the wine is not lesser but different: more Merlot, earlier picking, a shorter elevage and a style meant to be drunk sooner. Whether a buyer accepts that or reads it as a second wine with better marketing is exactly the argument the label was built to start.
